pieces.name: Document model & block identity
pieces.scope: ProseMirror schema shaped like OOXML; stable anchors that ride transactions
pieces.evidence: 5/5 identity tests pass: typing preserves anchors, split keeps identity on the first half, paste de-duplicates, delete is clean
pieces.gap: Not yet exercised against a real .docx-derived document.

pieces.name: App shell & host seam
pieces.scope: React chrome, ProseMirror surface, bun server implementing HostApi
pieces.evidence: The app runs. Real .md opened from disk, edited and saved back correctly — frontmatter, GFM table, ordered list, bold, em-dash, CJK and ± all survived. Live status bar reads 2.7 ms p99 keystroke latency in a real browser, including ProseMirror’s DOM write, against an 8 ms budget.
pieces.gap: Only the Markdown path is wired. Opening a .docx in the app is not possible yet, so the document-polish comparison against Google Docs cannot be run.

pieces.name: Markdown ⇄ model
pieces.evidence: 96.19% idempotent across 1,442 real corpus files (README/docs from major open-source repos), zero parse or serialize errors. 36 tests, 282k assertions.
pieces.gap: The 3.8% that fails is concentrated in nested-list indentation, blockquote nesting and repeated-asterisk emphasis — all real, all characterized.

pieces.name: docx import, sidecar & anchors
pieces.scope: Offset-recording XML index, fidelity sidecar, alignment-based re-anchoring
pieces.evidence: 288/288 real Word documents import without throwing. Mean text recovery 99.49%; 260/286 files recover ≥99.5% of every <w:t> in the source. The fidelity ledger is populated and honest: 791 degraded entries, 144 informational.
pieces.gap: Text inside text boxes and content controls is dropped — the worst file recovers only 64.5%. The ledger names it (327 inline-drawing-detached, 75 content-control-unwrapped) rather than hiding it.

pieces.name: Round-trip scorer & corpus
pieces.scope: Real-world .docx corpus, three-tier fidelity score, pandoc baseline
pieces.evidence: Three tiers over 288 files with a pandoc baseline, plus an anti-strawman control: pandoc scored against its OWN output reaches 0.9743, so it is self-consistent and simply does not preserve the user’s document. Independently re-verified outside the scorer, including that pandoc can read our exported files with the edit intact.
pieces.gap: T2 is entailed by T0 for scriv and is labelled as such in the report rather than counted as a second result.

pieces.name: Latency gate
pieces.scope: Keystroke budget enforced by a test that fails the build
pieces.evidence: Gate is green and enforced. Keystroke → state commit p99 0.36 ms against 8 ms; in-browser keystroke → DOM 2.4 ms; 50-page docx import p99 670 ms against 1200; throughput p99 1.28 ms/paragraph against 1.5.
pieces.gap: Keystroke → paint is still unmeasured, so the 16 ms end-to-end budget remains unproven.

pieces.name: Smart text ops
pieces.scope: Selection-aware surrounds, multi-cursor, motions, transpose, join, kill-line
pieces.evidence: 49 tests. Segmentation across English, German, Hindi and Japanese; selection-aware surrounds; expand/shrink selection; sentence and paragraph motions; Emacs kill ring; transpose, join, duplicate, move, delete-word. Verified live in the app: surrounds wrap and nest, kill-line works, expand-selection turns a caret into a range.
pieces.gap: Multi-cursor is not built, and it is the hardest piece — ProseMirror ships no multiple-selection model, so it needs a custom Selection subclass and a dispatcher that maps every command across ranges. Move-paragraph is covered by unit test but was not reproducible through the browser automation, so it is unverified live.

pieces.name: Prose IntelliSense
pieces.scope: Workspace symbol index, completions, Harper diagnostics over an LSP seam
pieces.evidence: Working in the app against a real workspace: typing "@sand" offers a citation key from refs.bib — a different file — with matched characters highlighted; "[[Instr" offers a heading from notes/method.md and closes the link. Workspace scan indexes Markdown and BibTeX in the background. 19 package tests, 116 across the repo.
pieces.gap: Harper diagnostics are still not wired, so there are no squiggles — half of the IntelliSense requirement is missing.

pieces.name: AI inline edit
pieces.scope: Cmd-K streaming rewrite as accept/reject diff; three-way merge; agent mode
pieces.evidence: The reconcile engine is built and proven: 19 tests. Applying the diff reconstructs the revision character-for-character on 174/174 edits over real documents. Suggestions render as the schema’s own tracked-change marks, so accept yields exactly the proposed text and reject restores the original exactly.
pieces.gap: Cmd-K is not wired into the app and no provider key is set in this environment, so the streaming path and the three-way merge with concurrent typing are unverified. The engine is proven; the feature is not yet usable.

pieces.name: Workspace & git
pieces.scope: Fuzzy open, search, diff and blame at sentence granularity
pieces.evidence: Sentence segmentation, alignment and word-level intra-sentence diff landed.
pieces.gap: File tree, fuzzy open and search not started; nothing measured.

pieces.name: docx export splice
pieces.scope: Edit the original zip rather than regenerate it
pieces.evidence: Verified through the app itself, not a bench: opened a real 247-paragraph Word document, changed one word, saved. Of 20 zip entries exactly ONE differs — word/document.xml. Styles, numbering, headers, footers, themes, fonts and media return byte-identical. Of 247 paragraphs exactly one changed. pandoc reads the result.
pieces.gap: Save writes the .docx in place. The Markdown source of truth and the .scriv sidecar are held in memory but not yet written alongside it, so closing the app loses the fidelity ledger for that document.

decisions.d: ProseMirror, used directly — not Tiptap, not Lexical
decisions.why: Pure decorations are load-bearing for AI diffs, diagnostics and blame. Lexical and Quill lack them; Tiptap's auto-schema fights the OOXML mapping.

decisions.d: Splice the original zip; never regenerate it
decisions.why: Turns 'how much OOXML can we model?' into 'how little must we touch?'. An unedited round-trip is byte-identical, and fidelity degrades only in proportion to what was actually edited.

decisions.d: Exact in-session, fuzzy only for externally-edited files
decisions.why: While the doc is open we observed every change, so identity needs no guessing. Sequence alignment is reserved for files edited by another tool — that split is what makes the problem tractable.

decisions.d: Drop formatting rather than risk misapplying it
decisions.why: A dropped style is a visible bug the writer can fix; a misapplied one silently corrupts a document they trusted.

decisions.d: harper.js in a worker, behind an LSP-shaped seam
decisions.why: Offline, Apache-2.0, works unchanged in web v1 and Tauri v2. The LSP shape makes adding a second checker cheap.

decisions.d: A measurement that covers only part of a path may fail a budget but may never certify a pass
decisions.why: A headless process cannot see the DOM half of a keystroke. Reporting it as 'pass' would manufacture confidence in a number that never measured the thing it names.

decisions.d: A tier entailed by another tier is labelled, not counted twice
decisions.why: Scriv’s T2 is 1.0000 because T0 is 100% — T2 scores the zero-edit round trip that T0 already proved byte-identical. Presenting both as achievements would inflate one fact into two.

decisions.d: A budget that names a size needs an upper bound on the band, and warm-up is reported separately rather than folded in
decisions.why: “50-page” measured as “≥500 paragraphs” swept in 11,000-paragraph documents and reported a failure three times the real one; a bench with no warm-up puts JIT cost in the p99 tail and blames the code for it.

decisions.d: Verified by pressing them in the running app, not by reading a table
decisions.why: Mod-Ctrl-ArrowUp looked ideal for expand-selection and is silently eaten by Mission Control on macOS. The keys the OS takes are now listed in the binding table so they are not rediscovered.

decisions.d: Every package is a referenced project, not just the ones that happened to be listed
decisions.why: Four packages including the largest were outside the root tsconfig references, so every clean typecheck was checking a subset. Adding them surfaced 114 errors, three of which were real defects.

decisions.d: The popup never opens on a bare word, at any length
decisions.why: Every threshold low enough to be useful is low enough to interrupt an ordinary sentence. Code completion can fire on every identifier character because a programmer is always naming something; a writer usually is not.

decisions.d: The gate will not fail on a percentile its own sample size cannot support
decisions.why: docx throughput measured 1.299, 1.841 and 2.281 ms across three runs of identical code. With 227 samples a p99 rests on about three order statistics. A gate that fails at random teaches people to re-run until it passes.

decisions.d: Rendered with the schema’s existing tracked-change marks, not a parallel mechanism
decisions.why: Accepting an AI rewrite and accepting a colleague’s tracked change become one code path, an AI suggestion exports to Word as a real revision, and undo and position mapping already understand it.

notes: The prose diff started at 5/174 on reconstructing real edits and reached 174/174 through three fixes, each a case where the tidier behaviour was the wrong one — most tellingly, word spans that absorbed their own spacing produced a cleaner diff that did not reproduce what the model actually returned.

The completion popup found three bugs by being used rather than read: accepting a citation produced “@@key” because the replacement range started after the sigil, the popup ran off the window edge, and the detail line printed an absolute filesystem path.

Entity detection without a stop-word list took three attempts against real documents. The top “entities” in a 40-document sample were initially Fix, Add, The and This — a capital is explained by position, and in reference documentation a closing bracket or dash explains one as completely as a full stop does.
A Word document now opens, edits and saves in the app, touching exactly one of its twenty zip parts. That is the hard requirement, demonstrated through the UI rather than a benchmark.

packages/ooxml, textops, workspace and perf were never in the typecheck graph. Every “typecheck clean” reported before this wave was checking five of nine projects and excluding the largest. Now all nine are referenced and clean.

Two bugs in the selection ladder were found by testing rather than reading: it walked back down once a selection spanned two paragraphs, and selecting the whole document used a position that sits between nodes rather than inside text. Both are now asserted by tests.

The perf gate went from red to green through three changes, only one of which was an optimisation: discarding warm-up (3352→2364 ms), bounding the 50-page band so it stopped including 500-page documents (→1260 ms), and removing per-part hashing that nothing read (→670 ms).

A check of mine reported three documents losing right-to-left run formatting. Reading the XML showed the opposite: the exporter had dropped a second, completely empty run carrying only that property and no text, which is correct. The comparison was wrong, not the exporter — it compared whole property payloads, which cannot tell a legitimate run merge from a real loss. It now compares property names, and that invariant is enforced by a test.

The splice design is validated: on real Word documents an unedited round trip is byte-identical, and a one-word edit changes exactly one paragraph. Pandoc, which regenerates, scores 0% on both — while remaining self-consistent at 0.9913 against its own output, so this is not a strawman: it preserves its own conversion faithfully, just not the user's document.

The gate is currently RED, deliberately and correctly: importing large Word documents takes p99 3.35s against a 1.2s budget. A 84ms average across the whole corpus had hidden this — the large documents are the bottleneck.

A status-bar reading that looked like two bugs turned out to be the 220 ms coalescing timer doing its job — the status store deliberately keeps typing off React’s render path. Verified by measurement rather than patched on suspicion.
Both session interruptions cost roughly a wave each. Builders now commit after every deliverable, which is why nothing was lost the second time.
The .docx corpus is public real-world documents. The 59 .docx files in ~/Downloads are personal and are deliberately not used.
